newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN STOCKS SEEN WEIGHED BY RESULTS TO MID-98.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN STOCKS SEEN WEIGHED BY RESULTS TO MID-98.

text.p: Recent poor corporate results, weighed by a slowing economy, will continue to drag on South African stock prices and a turnaround is unlikely before the middle of 1998, equity strategists said on Friday.

"I think corporate earnings are going to take a lot longer to recover and accelerate to the extent that we would like them to. I think most of the strategists conform that by the middle of next year we should see the corporate earnings picking up once again," said Dana Becker, equity strategist at ING Barings.

The rot started with leading retailer Edgars Ltd who last week reported a drop in year earnings to 598 cents per share from 642 cents, disappointing analysts who reached a consensus forecast of 638 cents.

In the wake of the news Edgars' share price plunged to a five-month low of 98 rand, weighed further by a warning that the next six months would be tight because of expected continued subdued economic activity.

Company earnings cannot be viewed seperately from the wider South African economic canvas as high interest rates and a slow down in the economy have, and will continue to, hit profit margins hard, strategists said.

"What's happening in the broader economy? High interest rates. There is a slow down taking place and if you translate that into corporate earnings you obviously get lower numbers," Becker told Reuters.
Consumer-related companies are and will remain hardest hit, strategists and dealers said, blaming high interest rates for curbing spending.
"The consumer side is obviously being hit very hard by high interest rates," Becker said.
But strategists said that share prices would not be hacked too mercilessly as many investment fund managers are looking through current hard times to a rosier future.

"I think quite a lot of fund managers are looking through the current bad earnings and are actually seeing some light on a 12 to 18 month horison and therefore not panicking out of the stocks," Becker said.
He added that investors were moving into quality stocks.

Since Edgars, a spate of disappointing results and profit warnings over the last two weeks from key industrial and retail companies -- including packaging company Nampak dgars and cement company PPC Ltd -- have hit related share prices hard.
"Some were discounted, some weren't. Some have really been a shock to the market. Companies like Nampak have surprised on the downside," Becker said.
Nampak on Monday reported fairly flat half-year earnings of 52.2 cents per share from 45 cents previously and cautioned that full year earnings were unlikely to improve.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange's retail stock index has lost more than five percent since May 6 and the industrial index more than two percent in the same period.
"We've not seen very good results at all," said Grahame Graham-Parker, general manager of Infinity Asset Management.
Ahead of its results, Nampak's share price fell from an intraday high of 19.75 rand on May 5 to a day low of 17 rand on May 13, the day after it reported.

"Results have been disastrous and sure we can absorb this, if we haven't already, but what about the next few months. There's little to hope for as far as improvement goes," said a stock market dealer.
Pretoria Portland Cement's (PPC) half-year earnings fell to 201.9 cents per share from 226.6 cents, shocking analysts who had forecast consensus earnings of 232.52 cents.
